text: He went back to his room. <break time="0.8s" /> And the scent of mignonette had gone. <break time="0.8s" /> Leaving only the stale, lifeless smell. <break time="0.8s" /> Of old furniture and storage. <break time="0.8s" /> The hope that had burned in him for five months. <break time="0.8s" /> Died at last. <break time="0.8s" /> And he sat staring at the dim yellow light. <break time="0.8s" /> For a long time. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, overcome by despair. <break time="0.8s" /> He gave up on life itself. <break time="0.8s" /> And he put out the light. <break time="0.8s" /> And lay down on the bed in the silent dark. <break time="0.8s" /> That night the housekeeper, Missus Purdy. <break time="0.8s" /> Sat in the basement with her friend Missus McCool. <break time="0.8s" /> And the two landladies shared. <break time="0.8s" /> A can of beer and some gossip. <break time="0.8s" /> I rented my third floor back. <break time="0.8s" /> This evening to a young man. <break time="0.8s" /> Said Missus Purdy. <break time="0.8s" /> And Missus McCool asked in surprise. <break time="0.8s" /> And did you tell him about it. <break time="0.8s" /> Rooms, said Missus Purdy. <break time="0.8s" /> Are furnished to be rented. <break time="0.8s" /> And I did not tell him. <break time="0.8s" /> And Missus McCool agreed. <break time="0.8s" /> That it was good business sense. <break time="0.8s" /> Missus McCool remembered the pretty young girl. <break time="0.8s" /> Who had ended her own life. <break time="0.8s" /> In that very room only a week before saying that she had a sweet little face. <break time="0.8s" /> She would have been called handsome, as you say. <break time="0.8s" /> Said Missus Purdy. <break time="0.8s" /> But for that mole. <break time="0.8s" /> She had by her left eyebrow. <break time="0.8s" /> Do fill your glass again.
